Free tools

Claude Code Subagent Check

Paste a .claude/agents/*.md subagent definition and get every structural mistake flagged in seconds — a name that isn't kebab-case, a description too vague for the orchestrator to delegate to it reliably, a tools entry that's empty, duplicated, or unrecognized, a model alias this tool doesn't know, and a missing or near-empty system prompt.

Structural checks, not a delegation test. This tool never runs your subagent and never calls an LLM — it only looks at the text you paste and flags known failure shapes in it. It does not know whether Claude Code's orchestrator will actually delegate to this subagent on a given request; it only tells you the file is well-formed enough to have a fair shot.

1. Paste your subagent definition

The full contents of the .md file, frontmatter and system prompt together. Nothing here is uploaded — everything runs in this page.

Findings

Paste a subagent definition above, or load the example, then press Check.

    Usage is optional, stays in this browser, and counts only that a check ran or a summary was copied. Nothing you paste — no subagent name, description, tools, or prompt text — is ever recorded, uploaded, or sent to an analytics service. Uncheck to turn it off. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control disable counting automatically.

    Common questions

    What does this tool check in a subagent definition file?

    The YAML frontmatter (name, description, tools, model) and the Markdown system-prompt body that follows it. Name: present, kebab-case, and matching the filename you give. Description: present and not too vague to trigger reliable delegation (length, a concrete trigger cue, distinctive vocabulary). Tools: no empty or duplicated entries, and each name checked against a documented list of built-ins as a caution. Model: checked against documented aliases and the shape of a full model id, also as a caution. Body: not missing or near-empty.

    Does this tool contact a network or Anthropic's servers?

    No. Every check is a deterministic, structural check against the text you paste, entirely in your browser. It never uploads anything and never calls an LLM.

    Does a clean result mean the orchestrator will delegate to my subagent correctly?

    No. This tool checks the shape of the file, not Claude Code's actual delegation decisions at runtime. A description can pass every heuristic here and still not get picked for a given request, and a description that trips a caution can still work fine in practice -- every finding is worth a look, not a verdict.

    Why is an unrecognized tool or model name only a caution, never an error?

    Because MCP tool names and custom tool names are open-ended, and Anthropic can add a new built-in tool or model alias at any time. This tool checks against a documented, dated reference list -- a name outside it is worth a second look for a typo, not proof of a mistake.

    No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not a guarantee of how Claude Code will delegate to or run this subagent, and it does not replace testing the subagent in the agent you actually run it in. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for checking any finding against Claude Code's current documentation. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

    Privacy. Everything runs client-side in your browser. The subagent text you paste, and every finding this tool produces, never leaves your device — there is no upload, no server-side processing, and no third-party analytics vendor.

    Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record.

    Checking Claude Code's own settings.json instead? See Claude Code Settings Check. Checking an agent Skill's SKILL.md instead? See Skill Manifest Check. Auditing an MCP server's launch config instead? See MCP Config Risk Check. Checking a pasted file for hidden or invisible Unicode instead? See Hidden Unicode Check. Checking a hook's command text for dangerous shapes instead? See Claude Code Hooks Security Check.

vs-reading-the-subagent-file-by-eye.html.text:
← Claude Code Subagent Check

Claude Code Subagent Check vs. reading the subagent file by eye

Reading a short subagent definition with an obviously empty tools list catches that list. It reliably misses a description that reads fine to a person but carries no trigger cue an orchestrator matches on, a duplicated tool name buried in a long comma-separated list, a name that doesn't match its own filename, and an unrecognized model alias that looks plausible — which is what this free, no-upload checker computes exactly, in one pass.

Where reading it yourself stops being enough

Anyone writing a subagent definition already does this: read the frontmatter and the prompt body and decide whether it looks right before trusting the orchestrator to pick it up. For a file with an obviously empty tools field, that read catches it. The problem is the other checks below are not the kind of thing a skim of readable prose and a comma-separated list reliably surfaces.

What you're trying to confirmReading the subagent file yourselfThis checker
The tools field isn't empty or missing.Works. This is the one case a plain read reliably catches.Also catches it, in the same pass as everything below.
The name field is kebab-case and matches the file's own filename.Two separate strings in two separate places; a rename to one and not the other is easy to miss.Compared directly, every time.
The description gives the orchestrator a concrete trigger cue, not just readable prose about what the subagent does."Handles code review" and "use PROACTIVELY when a PR is opened" both read as fine sentences to a person.Checked for length, a trigger-cue pattern, and distinctive vocabulary, the same way every time.
No tool name is duplicated, and every one is recognized, across a long comma-separated tools list.Read left to right for the names that matter; a repeat from copying a sibling's frontmatter doesn't stand out.Every entry compared against every other entry, and checked against a documented list.
The model alias is one this tool recognizes, as a caution against a typo.Requires recognizing the current set of aliases from memory.Checked against a dated reference list automatically.
The prompt body isn't missing or near-empty.Visible at a glance for an entirely blank body; a few thin sentences can still read as "something is there."Checked against a length threshold, every time.
Re-checking an entire subagent definition again after editing the frontmatter.Read start to finish again, remembered by hand.One paste, every field, every time.

A quick read is still the fastest way to catch an obviously empty field in a short file, and this checker is not doing anything a careful review couldn't — it is reading the same frontmatter and prompt body a careful review would, just checking every field against fixed rules automatically instead of judging the description's wording and comparing the tools list by eye.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: the browser page parses text you paste entirely in your own browser. It never sends your subagent definition anywhere.

Common questions

Can't I just read the subagent file myself?

For a file with an obviously empty tools list or a missing description, yes -- that case is visible on a single read. What reading does not reliably catch is a description that reads as perfectly good prose to a person but carries no concrete trigger cue an orchestrator matches on, a tool name duplicated inside a long comma-separated list, a name that doesn't match its own filename, or an unrecognized model alias that looks like a real one. Those need the same fixed checks run against the frontmatter every time, not judged by eye.

Why is a description that reads fine but won't trigger delegation hard to catch by eye?

Because "this subagent handles code review" and "use PROACTIVELY when a PR is opened" are both grammatically fine, readable sentences -- the difference is whether the wording gives the orchestrator a concrete condition to match a request against, not whether it reads well. A person skimming the frontmatter judges the sentence as prose; this tool checks it for length, a trigger-cue pattern, and distinctive vocabulary, the same way for every subagent.

Why is a duplicate tool name in a long list easy to miss?

A tools field with a dozen comma-separated names is read left to right for the names that matter, not compared entry by entry against itself. A name repeated once in the middle of the list -- often from copying and editing a sibling subagent's frontmatter -- does not stand out visually the way a missing or malformed field does.

What about a name that doesn't match its own filename?

The frontmatter's name field and the file's own filename are two separate strings in two separate places -- one inside the YAML block, one in the file browser or path -- and nothing forces a reader comparing them from memory to notice a mismatch, especially after a rename. This tool checks the two strings against each other directly.

Is this page making a live comparison against a tool or company?

No. This page describes a manual habit anyone writing a Claude Code subagent definition already has -- reading the frontmatter and prompt by eye before trusting it to be picked up. It names no competing product or company. The checker itself makes no network request of any kind: the browser page parses pasted text in your own browser, and nothing you paste is ever uploaded.

It is not a guarantee of how Claude Code will delegate to or run this subagent, and it does not replace testing the subagent in the agent you actually run it in. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for checking any finding against Claude Code's current documentation.
